title: Nonlocal wavefront shaping through complex media
authors: Yanis Trouyet, Neelan Gounden, Pedro Ornelas, Patrick Cameron, Andrew Forbes, Hugo Defienne
abstract: Wavefront shaping is a key technique for mitigating scattering in complex media, enabling advanced imaging and optical communication. Yet existing approaches are inherently local, requiring active correction elements - such as spatial light modulators or deformable mirrors - to lie directly in the optical path of the scattered light, which limits their integration into compact imaging systems. Here, we experimentally demonstrate nonlocal wavefront shaping using spatially entangled photon pairs. By applying a phase correction to a photon that never interacts with the scattering medium, we compensate for the distortions experienced by its entangled partner and restore their initial spatial correlations. Our approach physically decouples the wavefront correction from the scattering medium, paving the way for imaging through complex media in compact and otherwise inaccessible systems.
summary: This paper demonstrates nonlocal wavefront shaping by utilizing spatially entangled photon pairs to correct for scattering distortions in complex optical media. By applying phase corrections to one photon that avoids the scatterer, the system restores the spatial correlations of its entangled partner. This technique offers a pathway for compact imaging through otherwise inaccessible, highly scattering environments.
main_problem: The paper addresses the challenge of mitigating scattering in complex media for advanced imaging by overcoming the limitation of existing local wavefront correction techniques.
main_result: The authors successfully demonstrated nonlocal wavefront shaping using spatially entangled photon pairs, restoring spatial correlations in all tested scattering regimes.
method: Nonlocal wavefront shaping is achieved by applying a phase correction to one photon (idler) that bypasses the scattering medium to compensate for distortions experienced by its entangled partner (signal) passing through the medium.
model_or_system: The experiment uses spatially entangled photon pairs generated via SPDC and tests the technique across three regimes: low-order aberrations (PDMS), single-scattering (Parafilm), and multiple-scattering (simulations).
key_observables: Spatial Intensity Correlation Matrix G^(2)(r_i, r_s) and the central correlation value C_0, used to quantify the restoration of spatial correlations.
important_parameters: Scattering mean free path (l_s), number of active SLM macropixels (N), and the measured enhancement ratio (e.g., $\eta \approx 2.4$ or $\eta = 49.5$).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on the entanglement between photon pairs and the ability to physically decouple the wavefront correction from the scattering medium.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the experimental setup, showing restored $G^{(2)}$ projections under optimized vs. unoptimized conditions for aberrations and scattering media.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first establishing the problem of local correction, then detailing the nonlocal approach using entangled pairs, and finally presenting experimental results across low-order aberration, single-scattering, and multiple-scattering regimes.
why_interesting: This work is highly relevant to quantum optics and open quantum systems, as it uses quantum entanglement to engineer wave propagation through highly lossy and complex media, effectively bypassing the need for in-situ active elements.

(a) Spatially entangled photon pairs (810 nm) are generated via type-II spontaneous parametric down-conversion (SPDC) using a collimated 405 nm continuous-wave laser and a 1-mm β-barium borate (BBO) crystal. A 650 nm long-pass (LP) filter rejects the pump, and a polarizing beam splitter (PBS1) separates signal and idler photons. In the idler arm, a 4f system (L1 = 40 mm, L2 = 200 mm) images the crystal onto a spatial light modulator (SLM), which is Fourier-imaged onto a SPAD camera via a 4f setup (L6 = 100 mm, L7 = 100 mm) combined with lens L8 = 100 mm.
